walkthroughs.body_html:
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt.

Reactivity goes Cl > Br > I. So chlorine displaces bromine and iodine; bromine displaces only iodine.

Example: Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2. The mixture turns orange as bromine is released.

The block in the middle (iron, copper, zinc, nickel.) are transition metals. They are very different from group 1.

They have high melting points, are dense and strong, often form coloured compounds, can have multiple oxidation states (Fe2+ and Fe3+), and many are useful as catalysts.

Hydrogen has 1 outer electron like group 1, but it's a non-metal gas. It's usually drawn on its own at the top.

Helium has only 2 electrons but a full outer shell, so it's placed with the unreactive noble gases in group 0, not group 2.

options: Br2 + 2KCl -> 2KBr + Cl2
Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2
I2 + 2KCl -> 2KI + Cl2
I2 + 2KBr -> 2KI + Br2

Atoms get bigger across a period, making electrons easier to add but harder to remove.
Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays roughly constant, so electrons are held more tightly.
Mass is spread evenly throughout the entire atom including the electron shells.
Atoms across a period have more shells, pulling electrons closer.
Metal atoms themselves move to carry the current.
Metals contain naturally moving protons that act as charge carriers.
